summary: Describes known operational problems when DHCPv6 relays are used with prefix delegation, which can break delegation and cause routing failures. It sets out functional requirements for relays to avoid these problems.

plainLanguage.summary: When a middleman passes a message between your home router and the ISP, it must do so carefully, or you will not get the addresses you need.

subtitle: Rules for the DHCPv6 relay that sits between a customer router and an ISP's prefix delegation server.

tldr.problem: Relays that forward DHCPv6 prefix delegation between customers and an ISP's server behave inconsistently, which can drop messages, lose routes after a reboot, or leave delegated prefixes unreachable.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC names the "delegating relay", lists five observed problems, and sets general, routing, service continuity and operational requirements for it.
tldr.outcome: Operators using DHCPv6 prefix delegation with relays are advised to make sure these requirements are followed on their networks.

facts.label: Recommended default lease limit
facts.value: At least 8 active leases per client

today: RFC 8987 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It still stands as the set of requirements for delegating relays.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Many ISPs offering native IPv6 use a DHCPv6 relay in their Layer 3 customer edge device and a separate, central DHCPv6 server. RFC 8415 describes relays, but does not give all the requirements a relay needs to behave predictably in this setup.

Implementations vary, which leads to problems such as messages not being forwarded or delegated prefixes being unreachable. This RFC provides requirements for relays used with prefix delegation.

Routes injected from learned prefixes are out of scope. Multi-hop relaying is not affected: the requirements apply only to the relay co-located with the first-hop router.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISP hands out blocks of addresses through a middleman. Different middlemen act differently, so this document sets common rules.

sections.title: Delegating Relay and Topology
sections.content:
The RFC introduces the term delegating relay: a device that forwards DHCPv6 messages containing IA_PD and IAPREFIX options between client and server. It does not run a DHCPv6 server, and it is responsible for routing traffic for the delegated prefixes.

Examples given: a CMTS in CableLabs DOCSIS environments, and a BNG in a DSL access network that has no local DHCPv6 server function.

The topology has a PD client on the client network, the delegating relay on the downlink side, and the DHCPv6 server across the operator network on the uplink side. The relay forwards messages to the server by multicast or unicast, and provides the operator's Layer 3 edge for the client network.
sections.plainLanguage: The relay is the post office between your home and the ISP. It passes your requests along and also knows which road leads to your new address block.

sections.title: Problems Seen in Existing Relays
sections.content:
The RFC describes five problems seen in commercially available devices.

  • Messages not forwarded. If a relay already has a lease on a port and a new client sends a Solicit, the relay may drop it until a Release arrives or the lease times out. This hurts when a failed device is replaced.
  • Loss of state on reboot. Without persistent state, the relay cannot route to delegated prefixes until new DHCP messages rebuild it.
  • Multiple prefixes per client. Some relays support only one delegated prefix per DUID, so the other prefixes are unreachable.
  • Duplicate MAC addresses and DUIDs. Some relays drop messages from a second client with the same DUID on another interface. In networks that use MAC or DUID for authentication, enforcing uniqueness is a needed function, not a problem.
  • Forwarding loops. If the client loses its lease but the relay keeps the route, traffic bounces between them until the client is reprovisioned or the lease ages out.
sections.plainLanguage: Some middlemen throw away letters from a new neighbor, forget the map after a nap, or send mail back and forth in circles. These are the troubles the rules aim to prevent.

sections.title: General Requirements
sections.content:
The general requirements are numbered G-1 to G-9. The core ones:

  • The relay MUST forward messages both ways without changing their contents (G-1).
  • It MUST allow multiple prefixes for one client, including several in one IA_PD and several IA_PDs (G-2, G-3).
  • It SHOULD allow the same DUID to hold leases on more than one interface at once, unless DUID uniqueness is needed for network function or security (G-4).
  • The maximum prefixes per client and the maximum active delegations per port MUST be configurable (G-5, G-6). Supporting at least 8 active leases per client as the default is RECOMMENDED (G-7).
  • The relay MUST update lifetimes from the client's reply messages it forwards and expire prefixes only when the valid lifetime has elapsed (G-8), and MUST expire leases on a Release (G-9).
sections.plainLanguage: The middleman must pass notes along untouched, allow a family to have several address blocks, and let you give blocks back when you are done.

sections.title: Routing Requirements
sections.content:
The relay MUST keep a local routing table updated with leases and next hops, and remove the route when a prefix is released or expires (R-1). Routes and ingress filters MUST use the same prefix length as in the IA_PD (R-2, R-3).

It MUST provide a way to update ingress filters dynamically for anti-spoofing as described in BCP 38 (R-3). It MAY advertise delegated leases into a routing protocol, and must withdraw the route when the lease ends (R-4).

To prevent loops, it SHOULD have a configurable policy to drop looping packets on client-facing interfaces (R-5). Those are packets for a delegated prefix whose ingress and egress interface match; on multi-access links the link-layer addresses must match as well. An ICMPv6 Type 1, Code 6 error MAY be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The middleman keeps an up-to-date map of which address block lives where, and refuses to send a parcel straight back where it came from.

sections.title: Service Continuity and Operations
sections.content:
To keep delegations across restarts, the relay SHOULD implement DHCPv6 Bulk Leasequery (RFC 5460) or store active delegations in persistent storage (S-1). If a client's next-hop link-local address becomes unreachable, routes MUST be retained unless released or expired (S-2). The relay SHOULD implement Active Leasequery (RFC 7653) to stay in sync with the server (S-3).

Operationally, the relay SHOULD offer a way to view active delegated prefixes with client details (O-1) and to clear bindings for a lease, a client or a port (O-2). Using a time synchronization protocol on relays and servers is RECOMMENDED (O-3).
sections.plainLanguage: The middleman should write down its notes so a reboot does not make it forget, and give the operator tools to look at and clear those notes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 8213 and RFC 8415. If BCP 38 filtering is implemented, the rules must be updated dynamically as prefixes are leased.

RFC 8213 describes securing relay-to-server messages with an IPsec tunnel, and the RFC recommends that the delegating relay implement it. Not implementing G-6 may allow a resource depletion attack on the relay. The operational security practices of RFC 4778 are recommended. There are no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the line to the ISP private, and cap how many blocks can be handed out so no one can use up the middleman's memory.
